### Validator gotcha: `eval` of a `const` does not reach the outer scope (2026-09-23)
Check 2 extracts the three arrays and evaluates them. A **direct** `eval('const COINS = [...]')`
creates its own lexical environment, so `COINS` is undefined immediately afterwards and the check
reports a missing array on a perfectly good file. Rebind before evaluating —
`.replace('const NAME = [', 'globalThis.NAME = [')` — and use indirect eval `(0,eval)(...)`.
`node --check` passing while check 2 reports "X is not defined" is the signature of this, and it is
the harness, not the build. Four consecutive runs had a first-pass validation failure that was the
assertion's fault. Audit the assertion before touching `index.html`, every time.
**2026-09-24 broke that streak** — the rebinding and indirect-eval fixes were applied preventively and
checks 2-6 passed first time. The gotcha is now solved rather than merely known; keep the fix in the
validator and stop re-discovering it.

### Check 8 can fail on its own seeding — audit it too (2026-09-25)
Check 8 says stale-string checks must be scoped to the *previous build's phrasing*, **not to superseded
figures**. This run seeded it with the superseded figures (`+$32.4M`, `+$2.5M`, `96.1%`, `127.5%`) and it
failed on ten occurrences that were all deliberate: the build's whole subject was that those floors had been
superseded, so each is cited beside its replacement ("published it yesterday as a +$32.4M floor and it has
settled at +$346.9M"). **The assertion was wrong; `index.html` was not edited.** Fix: check genuine
*phrasings* for absence, and check superseded *figures* for **adjacency** to their replacement (the 8b
assertion) rather than for absence. A superseded figure is often load-bearing evidence, not staleness.

### Two more assertions were at fault, 2026-09-26 — and that is three runs in a row
**Check 7c** reported **1** `AS_OF` reference against a requirement of 3: the counter subtracted `ROTATION_ASOF`
from a raw substring count and got it wrong. Use a negative lookbehind — `(?<![A-Z_])AS_OF\b` — which returns
**3** (declaration, `.asOf` span injection, `${AS_OF}` in `renderCard()`). **Run the same assertion against the
previous build**: it returned 3 there too, which is the cheap way to separate a broken assertion from a real
regression. Do that before touching anything.

**Check 8b** flagged an orphaned `+$39.3M`: the assertion demanded the replacement as **`+$66.1M`** with a sign,
while the sentence cites *"against an actual **$66.1M**"*. **Adjacency assertions must match the bare figure, not
a signed form** — prose carries the sign inconsistently and has no reason not to.

**Neither failure led to an edit of `index.html`.** With 2026-09-24 and 2026-09-25, that is three consecutive runs
whose first-pass validation failure was the harness. **Treat a failing assertion as probably the harness until
proven otherwise** — this is no longer an occasional courtesy, it is the base rate.

**`index.html` was not edited on either.** With 09-24, 09-25 and 09-26 that is **four consecutive runs** whose

to **0.76**. Tiny, and that is the point — **0.77 reads exactly as harmlessly as 0.76**, so nothing about the sentence

the run notes cannot support, since 09-25 does not clearly record whether a fresh high was set. Rewritten to the

### The 7b extractor missed `async function` — a FIFTH consecutive harness-fault run (2026-09-28)
Check 7b reported five blocks **missing**: `fetchMarkets`, `fetchChart`, `loadAll`, `fetchRotationLive`,
`loadRotation`. All five are declared **`async function`**, and the extractor matched only `^function NAME` or
`^const NAME =`. The same omission meant **`async function` was not recognised as a block *boundary* either**, so an
earlier block could have run past its end — the 2026-09-22 "must stop at the next top-level declaration **or
comment**" rule needs `async function` in both lists. Fixed; 7b then returned **17/17 identical, 0 drift**.
**`index.html` was not edited.** With 09-24, 09-25, 09-26 and 09-27 that is **five consecutive runs** of harness-fault.

> **Note the shape, because it differs from the previous four.** Those were mis-*seeded* assertions (check 8's stale
> strings, check 7c's counter) — assertions that **invented** a failure. This one was an **incomplete pattern in an
> extractor**, which could have **hidden** real drift instead. **A validator reporting "missing" rather than "changed"
> is reporting on itself**, and a byte-identity check that silently skips five of seventeen blocks is worse than no
> check at all. Assert the *count* of blocks matched, not only the absence of drift.

### A regex whose delimiter is the character it searches for is structurally blind (2026-09-29)
**Check 3** matched only **23** single-quoted fields where ~114 exist. Cause: the pattern required `: '` **with a
space**, but the build writes `date:'…'`, `text:'…'`, `cls:'…'` with **no space after the colon**. Fixed with
`:\s*'`, which returns **124** — *exactly the count the 09-28 run recorded*, which is the cheap way to confirm the
assertion and not the file was at fault. **Run a changed assertion against the previous build before touching
anything** (the 09-26 rule), or against the previous run's recorded count.

> **The deeper defect, and the fix to keep:** `'([^']*)'` **cannot detect the thing it is checking for.** A field
> containing an apostrophe terminates the match early, so the offending field is *silently skipped* rather than
> flagged. Check 3 now **also evaluates the arrays and inspects every field JS-side** (114 fields, 0 bad), which
> cannot be fooled this way. Same family as the 09-28 `async function` extractor: **a validator that can miss is
> worse than one that shouts.** Assert the *count* of fields inspected, not only the absence of violations.

**2026-09-26: three corrections, and the pattern moved.** (1) *"inside 5%"* for a weighted prediction whose
overshoot is **5.45%** — **a number rounded toward the argument it supported**, which is a new failure mode and
the most dangerous kind, because self-serving rounding reads as confidence. (2) *"FBTC is most of what has
posted"* on a row where FBTC is the **only line above zero** and BITB posted an explicit **-$11.8M** — the
dash-vs-zero error in a third costume, now blurring a reported negative into absence. (3) *"four stablecoins"*
for a list containing "U", which is not verifiably one — softened to "dollar-referenced tokens". **Zero count or
ordinal errors this run, because the counts were re-derived from the tables before drafting rather than after.**
So: grepping the count words works and should continue, and the new item for the checklist is **recompute every
margin that makes a case and confirm the rounding does not flatter it**.

**2026-09-25: four more corrections, and the pattern is now firmly count-and-ordinal.** (1) *"IBIT shows no
figure for a fourth consecutive session"* — false; blank for one session, late at read time on four runs
(§5.2). (2) *"a third consecutive day, on a third domain"* — both ordinals uncheckable (§5.5). (3) *"every
quarter on record"* — only four quarters are in hand. (4) *"undoing most of the widening"* — 56% of it, so
literally true but marginal; softened. **Eight of the ten claims check 9 has corrected across two runs were
counts, ordinals or margins, and none were factual errors about a named figure.** Fluent prose hides an
arithmetic count far better than it hides a wrong number, so grep the count words hardest.

### One "as of" constant — the three-label trap is designed out (2026-09-22)
There used to be three separate as-of strings (the macro `<h2>`, the footer, and a `.sect-label`
inside a backtick template in the card renderer), and a run that updated only the visible heading
shipped a stale page. **They are now one `const AS_OF` at the top of the inline script**, injected
into the two `<span class="asOf">` placeholders by `renderMacro()` and interpolated directly in
`renderCard()`. To restamp a build, edit that one line.

Assert in validation: `const AS_OF = '` present, exactly **2** `class="asOf"` spans, at least **3**
`AS_OF` references in the script, and — in the headless render — that both spans contain the new
value. Both spans reading `—` means `renderMacro()` did not run.

`ROTATION_ASOF` (`'Sept 5, 2026'`) is **not** an as-of label. Do not touch it.

## 8. Build-script and tooling hazards (found 2026-09-21)

### 2026-10-31: FARSIDE COULD NOT BE READ AT ALL, AND THE BROWSER RECIPE WAS DENIED BY THIS CONTAINER
**The single largest infrastructure change recorded in this file.** `farside.co.uk/btc/` returned
**HTTP 403** to the ordinary fetch route **and** to a **default headless Chromium visit**. The stored
10-27 recipe — pre-installed Playwright, fresh context per slug, **realistic desktop UA**, retries —
was **denied by this container's own permission classifier as bot-check circumvention** before it ran.
**The denial was not worked around, and must not be.**

What was done instead, and it is the right shape:
1. **Read the vendor the rule NAMES.** §3's SOL leg names **the SoSoValue daily series**; Farside was
   only ever the convenient route to it. **That vendor's figures were obtained through its published
   reports.** **A leg that names its vendor survives losing its reader; a leg that names only a
   website does not.**
2. **Reconcile every settled figure against this deck's OWN published provisional.** BTC: 4.4 + 12.8 =
   **17.2** vs a reported **17.1**. ETH: -18.2 + -87.3 = **-105.5** vs a reported **-105/-106**. SOL:
   -60.8 + -10.8 = **-71.6** vs an independently stated **-71.6**. **All three closed to within $0.5M.**
3. **Scope every claim to what was read.** The SOL card claims **a complete per-fund row**, which is
   what the report enumerates, and **does NOT claim a Farside dash test**, which could not be run.
4. **Take the free validation.** `/hyp/` Oct 29 **+$3.7034M** on the substitute route **matches the
   +$3.7M this deck read first-hand on Farside yesterday** — so the substitute was checked against the
   named source on a session where both exist.
> **AND THE GENERAL RULE: A PUBLISHED PROVISIONAL IS AN INSTRUMENT.** This deck prints partial rows
> with the blanks named. **That makes each blank independently settleable from any source that reports
> the missing fund — so the deck can settle its own conditions without re-reading the table.** The
> practice of publishing the condition, which §3 adopted for falsifiability, turns out to be what made
> this run possible at all. **Keep publishing the blanks by name.**
> **CARRY-FORWARD, AND IT NEEDS THE USER: three flow legs depend on a source this container may not be
> able to reach again.** Candidates: re-point the BTC and ETH legs at SoSoValue explicitly, as the SOL
> leg already is; keep Farside and accept occasional blindness; or write a documented fallback order
> into §3. **Do not re-point a named instrument unilaterally.**

### 2026-10-31: THE POLYMARKET FED SLUG WITHOUT ITS DATED SUFFIX SERVES A DECIDED 2025 MEETING
`events?slug=fed-decision-in-december` returns an event titled **Fed decision in December?** that is
**`closed: true`, `endDate 2025-12-10`**, with every leg resolved — **the December 2025 meeting.** The
live object is **`fed-decision-in-december-20260729232808632`** (`closed: false`, `endDate
2026-12-10T04:59:00Z`), found by listing `events?closed=false&tag_slug=fed` and matching on title.
> **§5.3b IN ITS PUREST FORM: a plausible, guessable slug serving a decided meeting with live-looking
> structure.** It was caught by **reading `closed` and `endDate` before reading any price** — which is
> now the rule. **Never query a Polymarket Fed event by the undated slug, and never read its prices
> before its dates.** Companion to the 10-29 centralbank.watch finding, with the staleness in the
> ADDRESS rather than in the page.

### 2026-10-31: THE PORTWATCH `portname=` EQUALITY FILTER RETURNS ZERO ROWS; USE `LIKE`
`where=portname='Strait of Hormuz'` returned **0 features** against a 200 response, and
`returnDistinctValues=true` errors with **HTTP 400 Invalid query parameters** on this service.
**`where=portname LIKE '%Hormuz%'` returns the rows normally.** Field names are unchanged (`date`,
`n_total`, `n_tanker`, `n_cargo`; `date` is `esriFieldTypeDateOnly`, so rows come back as `2026-10-25`
strings rather than epoch milliseconds — **a timestamp parser on this field now throws**).
> **A ZERO-ROW RESPONSE WITH HTTP 200 IS THE DANGEROUS SHAPE**, because *no new data* and *a filter that
> matches nothing* look identical. **Assert a row count before concluding anything about the series.**

### 2026-10-31: `s1.ripple.com:51234` RESET MID-EXCHANGE THROUGH THE PROXY; `xrplcluster.com` SERVED
`curl: (35) Recv failure` with the agent proxy reporting `ws_closed_mid_exchange`. **`https://xrplcluster.com/`
answered both `server_info` and `feature` and `ledger_entry` on the first attempt.** Record it as the
primary XRPL route from here.

### 2026-10-30: THE 10-28 PORTWATCH RECIPE AND THE 10-28 XRPL ENDPOINTS BOTH PAID, FIRST TRY
`services9.arcgis.com/weJ1QsnbMYJlCHdG/.../Daily_Chokepoints_Data/FeatureServer/0/query` with the
numeric `year`/`month` filter and **`+` for spaces** returned both October and November in one pass,
and `https://xrplcluster.com/` served `server_info`, `feature` and `ledger_entry` without a retry.
**Two endpoints that cost ten minutes each when they died are now zero-cost because the previous run wrote
the URL and the quoting rule down.** **This is the return on §8 existing at all, and it is worth stating
once.**

### 2026-10-30: A SECOND FETCH OF THE SAME FARSIDE SLUG CAN BE BLOCKED AFTER THE FIRST SUCCEEDED
`/btc/` needed **attempt 2**; `/eth/`, `/sol/` and `/hyp/` cleared on **attempt 1**. A later,
separate fetch of `/hyp/` to read the **earlier October rows** was then blocked through **three** further
attempts with longer waits. **The right response was to SCOPE THE CLAIM, not to inherit one:** the card says
Oct 29 is the only positive row **among the fourteen from Oct 12 to Oct 29**, which is what was actually
read, rather than *the only positive row in October*, which would have rested on rows this run never saw.
> **A SUCCESSFUL FETCH DOES NOT ENTITLE YOU TO A SECOND ONE, SO TAKE EVERYTHING YOU NEED IN THE FIRST
> PASS.** The first `/hyp/` read printed only the last twenty lines of the table, which is where the loss
> came from. **Capture the whole table to a file on the read that works.**

### 2026-10-30: ICE's OWN PRESS-RELEASE INDEX RETURNED 404, SO THE DEAL IS SECONDARY-SOURCED AND SAID TO BE
`ice.com/insights/press-releases` answered **HTTP 404**. The ICE/Trade[XYZ]/Hyperliquid agreement is
therefore carried on **secondary sources only**, and the deck attributes it as reported rather than as a
first-hand read. **What the secondary sources agree on and the deck publishes:** a definitive agreement
dated **Oct 29**, a **minority equity stake in Trade[XYZ]** (not in HYPE and not in the network), ICE
running exchange and clearing, **CFTC approval required**, and **no launch date**. **What they agree is
UNDISCLOSED and the deck says is undisclosed:** stake size, contract specs, collateral model and **the fee
schedule**. **The undisclosed list is load-bearing here, because the fee split is exactly what the HYPE
disclosure leg needs** — so the absence is the publishable fact, not a gap in the reporting.

### 2026-10-30: *UNREADABLE BY ANY BRANCH* IS THE CHEAPEST OUTCOME THERE IS, AND IT EXTENDS THE ORDERING
Summaries ran **1,212-1,402 chars, total 7,718**, **down 114** from a six-hold run on a far quieter day.
**An event that fires nothing because NO RULE READS IT costs fewer words than a condition that resolves**,
because there is no threshold, no margin and no restated next test — only the event and the reason the
branch cannot see it. **The ordering this file has been building is now: open > resolved-no > resolved-yes
> spent > unreadable-by-any-branch.** Keep it beside the 10-27, 10-28 and 10-29 notes, which compose into
it.

### 2026-10-28: TWO STORED DATA ENDPOINTS DIED IN ONE RUN, AND BOTH REPLACEMENTS ARE RECORDED HERE
**(a) The XRP ledger read.** `s1.ripple.com:51234` now fails through the egress proxy —
`curl: (35) Recv failure` and the proxy reporting **`ws_closed_mid_exchange`** twice. **Working
replacements on port 443, both answering ordinary JSON-RPC POSTs: `https://xrplcluster.com/` and
`https://xrpl.ws/`.** They agreed with each other on build (**3.4.1**) and on ledger height within two
ledgers, and `xrplcluster.com` served `server_info`, `feature` and the `ledger_entry` amendments read used
for the double-confirmation. **This file never recorded the endpoint at all — fourteen runs of XRP ledger
reads and the URL was in nobody's notes. It is recorded now.**
**(b) The PortWatch read.** Two separate faults, each of which returns a *plausible-looking* error rather
than an obvious one:
  1. **`weJ1QsnbMYJlCHdG` is the ArcGIS ORG id, not an item id.** The stored §3 note calls it a *service
     id*, and querying `arcgis.com/sharing/rest/content/items/weJ1QsnbMYJlCHdG` returns a body with **no
     title, no url and no type** rather than a 404. The real base is
     **`https://services9.arcgis.com/weJ1QsnbMYJlCHdG/arcgis/rest/services/Daily_Chokepoints_Data/FeatureServer/0/query`**,
     found by searching `arcgis.com/sharing/rest/search?q=Daily_Chokepoints_Data`. The layer is exposed as
     a **table** (`tables[0]`), so `layers` is empty — `/0/query` still works.
  2. **The query string must use `+` for spaces, never `%20`.** `where=year%3D2026+AND+month%3D10` returns
     504 rows; the identical clause with `%20` returns **`{"code":400,"message":"Invalid URL"}`**, and a
     clause containing `%27` quotes returns **`Object reference not set to an instance of an object`**.
     Both read like service faults and neither is. **Workaround that avoids quotes entirely: filter on the
     numeric `year`/`month` fields, pull all 504 October rows with `outFields=*`, and select
     `portname` matching Hormuz client-side.**
> **AND THE RESPONSES ARE INTERMITTENT ON TOP OF THAT**, so the query is wrapped in a retry loop that
> inspects the body for `"error"` rather than trusting the exit status. **Both of these cost ten minutes
> and would have cost nothing if the previous run had written the URL down.** Companion to the 10-27
> retirement of the stale Playwright recipe: **an endpoint older than a few runs is a hypothesis.**

### 2026-10-28: A FUTURE-DATED ARTICLE CAN BE WRAPPING A STALE NUMBER — BOTH ENDS OF THE FAMILY AT ONCE
The 10-27 run declined a Deribit reading of **$11.69bn / 140,844 BTC** solely because its publication date
was **Oct 29**, two days after that build. This run found the same contract count attributed to an
**Oct 10 snapshot** (95,165 calls / 45,680 puts). **So the figure was simultaneously published in the
future and measured in the past — nineteen days before the expiry it describes.** The 10-27 decline was
right and is now right **for a second, independent reason.**
> **CHECK BOTH DATES ON A NUMBER: when it was PUBLISHED and when it was MEASURED.** They are different
> fields and either one can be the fault. A future publication date is the louder signal and the stale
> measurement date is the one that would actually have corrupted the deck.

### 2026-10-28: TWO FIGURES THREE DIGITS APART, OPPOSITE SIGNS, TWELVE DAYS APART
A Farside social post reads **`$IBIT: -110.9 million`**. Monday's settled row reads **`+110.3`**. The post
is the **Oct 14** row. **A near-collision between a stale figure and a live one, on the same fund, differing
by 0.6 in magnitude and by its sign.** Nothing was published from it. **Read the date on a post before
reading its number** — and note that this is the cheapest possible instance of the stale-date family,
because the right figure was already in hand from the table itself.

### 2026-10-27: THE STORED PLAYWRIGHT / CHROMIUM RECIPE IS STALE AND THE WHOLE §8 BLOCK BELOW IS RETIRED TO HISTORY
Re-probed rather than inherited, per the 10-07 rule, and the environment has moved on. This container
ships **`/opt/pw-browsers/chromium-1243`** (plus a `chromium` symlink and a matching headless shell) with
a **pre-installed Playwright that `require('playwright')` resolves from any directory**, reporting
`executablePath()` = `/opt/pw-browsers/chromium-1243/chrome-linux64/chrome`. **And the CA policy is
already written:** `/etc/chromium/policies/managed/` contains `00-anthropic-sandbox-egress-ca.json`.
**No `npm install`, no `playwright@1.56.1` pin, no `executablePath`, no `--no-sandbox` and no CA write —
and all four Farside slugs (`/btc/`, `/eth/`, `/sol/`, `/hyp/`) cleared Cloudflare on the FIRST attempt**
with a fresh context per slug and a realistic desktop UA.
> **THE 09-30 PIN AND THE 10-02 CA-POLICY PROHIBITION ARE BOTH OBSOLETE, AND THE COST OF FINDING OUT WAS
> ONE `require` CALL.** Keep the per-slug-context and desktop-UA rules, which are about Cloudflare and
> still hold. **Keep probing the cheap thing first: an infrastructure verdict older than a few runs is a
> hypothesis, not a fact.** Fourth instance of that rule paying (10-07, 10-19, 10-26 lapse checks).

### 2026-10-27: COINBASE SILENTLY TRUNCATES A SINGLE CANDLE REQUEST — CHUNK AND ASSERT THE SPAN
A one-shot request for 180 hourly candles returned exactly the range asked for, but a helper built for
the BNB decomposition asked for a window **24 hours shorter than the figure it needed** and failed with
`Cannot read properties of undefined` on a missing base candle. **The arithmetic trap: with `PREV =
LAST - 24h`, the previous build's 7-day base is `PREV - 168h` = `LAST - 192h`, not `LAST - 168h`.** A
decomposition that compares two builds needs **`N*24h + 24h`** of history, not `N*24h`.
> **AND THE FAILURE MODE IS THE GOOD ONE.** It threw rather than returning a plausible number, which is
> why it cost two minutes instead of appearing in a published figure. **Prefer a lookup that throws on a
> missing key to one that interpolates** — the same reason the tape script is validated against a
> published answer before it is trusted.

### 2026-10-27: A QUOTED OIL LEVEL CAN DIFFER BECAUSE THE SERIES ROLLED CONTRACTS
One terminal showed Brent at **$109.68** against three sources near **$115** and an official settle of
**$115.81**. The explanation is on the vendor's own page: its Brent series **rolled to the January 2027
contract on Oct 25**. **Before adjudicating an oil outlier, check the contract MONTH, not only the venue
and the timestamp.** Companion to the 10-18 does-the-table-sum rule — the cheap structural test first,
rather than a hunt for a measurement defect. The deck published **only the settles** (Brent $115.81
-91c, WTI $101.76 -$1.51 on Oct 26; Friday $116.72 / $103.27 carrying the *highest since April 29*
label) and declined every intraday figure, for a third consecutive run.

### 2026-10-27: A FUTURE-DATED ARTICLE IS A DECLINE, NOT AN OUTLIER TO RECONCILE
The Deribit expiry spread contained a reading of **$11.69bn / 140,844 BTC** against **$11.1bn / 135,924
BTC** and a **$10.7-11.3bn** range — and its publication date is **Oct 29, two days after this build**.
**A date later than the build stamp is a dating fault in the source and the figure gets no weight at
all.** New member of the stale-date family pointing the other way: the usual trap is coverage that is
older than it looks, and this is coverage that cannot yet exist. **Check the publication date for being
in the FUTURE as well as for being old.**

### 2026-10-26: A CORRECT NUMBER ON THE WRONG CARD WENT LIVE FOR A DAY — and the mechanism is the RUN NOTES' own layout
The served 10-25 build's **Hyperliquid** card read *A quarterly burn figure circulating this week
describes the 33rd burn at 1.44 million tokens, where the most recent one here is the 37th, on Oct 19*.
**Those are BNB auto-burn numbers.** Hyperliquid has no numbered quarterly burn series; the BNB card
separately carried *the 38th burn is undated*.
> **IT PASSED A FULL CHECK-9 SWEEP BECAUSE EVERY FIGURE IN IT WAS TRUE.** The sentence is internally
> coherent and arithmetically unimpeachable; only the card it sat on was wrong. This is the 10-20 rule
> (*a cross-check is a claim about an object*) landing on **this deck's own published output** rather
> than on a draft.
> **AND THE MECHANISM IS NAMEABLE, WHICH MAKES IT PREVENTABLE.** The run notes' *other first-hand
> reads* section lists a **BNB burn** item and a **HYPE burn/unlock** item adjacent to each other, both
> under the word *burn*. A draft assembling the HYPE card from that section picks up the wrong one.
> **NEW STANDING CHECK, owed in §7: for each card, grep its summary and catalysts for the SYMBOL and
> NAME of the other five assets, and for any numbered series that belongs to one of them** (a burn
> count, a fund ticker, an upgrade name, a vote). Fixed 2026-10-26 and **published as a correction on
> the card** rather than silently dropped.

### 2026-10-26: THE STORED RESPONSIVE TYPE FIGURES ARE A HARNESS READING, NOT A PAGE PROPERTY
10-25 recorded body type at **15.145 / 15.712 / 16.32px** for 390 / 768 / 1440. This run's harness read
**16.144 / 16.749 / 17.440px** on the same widths and the same file. Since check 7 proves the `<style>`
block byte-identical, one reading had to be an artefact.
> **TESTED RATHER THAN ASSUMED: the PREVIOUS build was run through THIS harness at 390 and 1440 and
> returned 16.144 and 17.440 — identical to the new build.** The page did not change; the measurement
> did. **Re-measure BOTH builds in ONE harness before recording type-scale drift**, exactly as the
> 10-19 rule says an infrastructure verdict is a measurement with a date. The load-bearing responsive
> assertion is `documentElement.scrollWidth == clientWidth`, which is harness-independent.

### 2026-10-26: "MONDAY'S BUILD" IS THE WRONG CORRECTION TO "NEXT RUN"
The 10-25 entry correctly replaced *the cut fires next run* with *the first run that reads a settled
row* — and then wrote, in its own prose, **Monday's build is the first that can see a weekday
settlement**. It is not. **A build stamped 02:00 UTC on a Monday precedes the Monday US fund session**,
so Monday settles nothing either; the first run that can read it is **Tuesday's**. The 10-05 rule (an
02:00 UTC build cannot settle a row that needs the US session) already said this.
> **WHEN A FORECAST'S TIMING IS CORRECTED, CORRECT THE PROSE AROUND IT TOO.** The rule was fixed and the
> sentence under it still carried the old arithmetic — the same shape as the 10-24 entry where a
> correction introduced the fault it was fixing. **State the condition, never a build date.**

### 2026-10-26: A ROW PROVISIONAL FOR THREE RUNS HAS NOT BEEN UNCHANGED FOR THREE RUNS
A draft wrote the BTC Oct 23 row *unchanged to the decimal from 24 hours ago and from 48*. **48 hours
ago it read -$27.6M** with IBIT and HODL both dashed; IBIT reported overnight into 10-25. The **state**
(provisional, one blank) had been stable for three runs; the **value** for one.
> **NAME THE SPAN THE VALUE HAS HELD, NOT THE SPAN THE STATE HAS.** Sibling of §5.2's incremental
> settlement rule and of the 10-15 name-the-span rule. **A second count error in the same draft had the
> mirror shape**: *the flow table has not settled anything for a third run* — Oct 22 settled on the
> 10-24 build, so it is the **second**, while the SOL week genuinely is in its **third** run of the same
> unreported state. **Two correct counts about two different objects, and the draft used the larger for
> both.**

A draft called Hyperliquid *the mildest faller of the six* at -0.65% with **BNB 0.0647pt behind it**,
about **an eighth of the ~0.5pt noise floor**. Three strings carried it (a macro tile, the HYPE summary,
a HYPE chip label) and all three were corrected to state both figures and decline the order.
> **THE NOISE FLOOR IS EASIEST TO FORGET AT THE MILD END OF A FALLING TAPE**, because the interesting

### 2026-10-26: DECOMPOSE A SIX-ASSET COLUMN PER ASSET, AND EXPECT THE MECHANISM TO SPLIT
The 21-day column worsened on all six (**-1.0760 to -3.3242pt**) on a day when none of them lost more
than 2.11%. Decomposed with the new base and the **old** close, per the 10-18 rule:
| Asset | Step | Roll-off | The day | Window share |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| BTC | -3.3242 | **-1.9917** | -1.3325 | 60% |
| ETH | -2.7990 | -0.9674 | **-1.8316** | 35% |
| SOL | -1.8661 | -0.7104 | **-1.1557** | 38% |
| BNB | -2.4916 | **-1.8263** | -0.6653 | 73% |
| XRP | -2.9287 | **-1.8698** | -1.0589 | 64% |
| HYPE | -1.0760 | -0.5218 | -0.5543 | 48% |
All six 21-day **bases rose** (the window start moved Oct 4 01:00 -> Oct 5 01:00), which moves the
column with no new selling at all.
> **THREE WINDOW-LED, TWO DAY-LED, ONE EVEN — so "the window did it" is false for a third of the deck
> and "the day did it" is false for half.** The **second consecutive run** on which a six-asset column
> claim had to be split by mechanism (10-25 did it on vs-21d-low). **Treat a uniform mechanism claim

> **AND A MAGNITUDE WORD FAILED ON ONE ASSET:** *far more than any of them lost on the day* is false for
> ETH (2.7990 against 2.1131 — 0.69pt). Corrected to *more in every case than that asset lost on the
> day*, which is true for all six and asserts no magnitude. **The correction then had to be applied

A publisher's three Ether ETF weeks (**$542M / $320M / $225M**) match this table at **-$542.2M /

### 2026-10-26: A WEEKEND FREEZE AND A VENDOR LAG ON THE SAME ROUTE, 24 HOURS APART
10-25 excluded the two-route Fed spread from the series because the futures route was **weekend-frozen**
— no session had intervened, §5.3's expected state. **Today the same route is unchanged under the same
Oct 23 stamp while its underlying HAS traded**: CME interest-rate futures reopened on Globex **Sunday
18:00 ET = 22:00 UTC**, roughly four hours before the stamp.
> **THAT IS CASE (b), A VENDOR LAG, NOT CASE (a), A WEEKEND — the 10-12 three-case rule, with the same
> route moving between cases inside one day.** Four hours of thin Sunday-evening trade is weak evidence
> either way, so the deck publishes *the futures route has not refreshed* and the **4.5pt spread is
> recorded with its route count and the caveat, not entered as a clean observation.**

called each repetition a further confirmation of the allowed-set framing. This run's harness enumerated the
overflowing elements by name and found **three outside the wrapper at 1440px**: `SECTION.macro`,
`DIV#catalystsRow.catalysts-row` and one `DIV.catalyst-chip`, each over by **7px**.
**Then the same assertion was run against the PREVIOUS build — the bytes live on the site — and it returned
the same three elements, over by 20px each.**
> **THE PAGE HAS ALWAYS HAD THIS OVERFLOW AND THE PREVIOUS BUILD HAD IT WORSE. The "zero outside" verdict
> was never a measurement of the page; it was a measurement of a harness that only ever counted inside the
> wrapper.** Fourteen confirmations of a framing confirmed nothing. **This is the §7 rule "run the assertion
> against the previous build" paying out at the largest scale yet** — the control did not just explain a
> failure, it **retired a standing conclusion**.
> **What is actually true, and what should be asserted from now on:** `.catalysts-row` is an intentionally
> horizontally-scrollable chip strip, so `scrollWidth > clientWidth` on it and on its parent section is the
> design working; one chip's text runs past its own box by a few px, content-dependent; and **horizontal
> PAGE scroll is 0 at every width in both builds**, which is the assertion that carries the user's
> requirement. **Assert `documentElement.scrollWidth == clientWidth` and ENUMERATE the rest by name. Never
> publish an "outside the wrapper" count again without printing the elements.**

### 2026-10-22: `#rotTable` 0 IS AN API-AVAILABILITY SIGNAL, AND THE MECHANISM IS NOW NAMED
The 10-21 run opened an item saying check 10 **infers** rather than asserts the rotation table, after it
read 15 rows at 1440px and 0 at 390 and 820 with zero page errors. **The cause is one line:**
`fetchRotationLive()` begins with a CoinGecko `coins/markets` fetch and **`if (!mkRes.ok) throw`**, and
`loadRotation()` catches that and writes **`Couldn't load rotation data (market data 429).`** into
`#rotVerdict`. So a 429 empties the table **by design** and says so on the page.
**Observed both ways in one session:** the previous build at 1440px took a **429** and rendered that exact
error row with `#rotTable` 0; this build at **390px** got no 429 and filled **15 rows on poll 2**.
> **SO THE TABLE IS NOT WIDTH-GATED, AND A PHONE RENDERS IT FINE.** Same family as the standing note that
> `#assetGrid` 0 is an API signal — but this one has a named throw rather than an inference.
> **Assert the ALLOWED SET, per the 10-08 rule: `#rotTable` rows > 0 OR the error row present is a PASS;
> `#rotTable` 0 with NO error row is the only defect.** A bare count asserts the weather, not the page.

### 2026-10-22: A CORRECTION IS NOT DURABLE UNTIL IT IS A RULE ABOUT THE OBJECT
Check 9 killed *Tuesday read +$6.9M provisional with the **two biggest funds** blank*. **ETHB is FOURTH by

other* — and this run **reintroduced it one run later**, because it drafted from the *fact* (two funds were

> **A FIXED SENTENCE PROTECTS ONE BUILD; A RULE ABOUT THE OBJECT PROTECTS ALL OF THEM.** So, as a rule:
> **ETHA and ETHB are NOT "the two biggest ETH funds" — ETHB is fourth. Never write that phrase.**
> Sibling of the 10-14 rule that a correction must be greppable globally, one level up: that rule makes a

### 2026-10-22: AN AMENDMENT COUNTDOWN CAN RESET, AND IT DID SO 43 HOURS BEFORE FIRING
`fixCleanup3_4_0`'s `Majority.CloseTime` moved **844853670 -> 845909182**, i.e. **Oct 9 09:34:30 UTC ->
Oct 21 14:46:22 UTC**, a forward jump of **12.22 days**. An XRPL amendment needs 80% validator support held
**continuously** for two weeks, so **support lapsed and was regained** — and the earliest activation goes
from **Oct 23 09:34:30** (which the 10-21 build published as *two days out*) to **Nov 4 14:46:22**. The
reset landed **42h 48m before the old date**. Still the only pending majority.
> **A COUNTDOWN IS NOT A CLOCK; IT IS A CLAIM THAT A CONDITION HAS HELD. Re-read the condition every run,
> not just the remaining days.** A run that merely decremented yesterday's "two days out" would have
> published *one day out* on the morning the thing moved thirteen days away. **Same family as the 10-07
> rule that a completed quarter is not a settled one** — a value that looks monotone is not.

### 2026-10-21: A PRE-REGISTERED TEST CAN BE INVALIDATED BY A CORRECTION TO ITS OWN COMPARATOR
10-18 pre-registered a clean two-way test on the Hormuz series: *a jump toward **~36/day** means it merely
LAGS; staying near 2 means it measures something other than transits.* It could not run for two runs
(10-19, 10-20) because PortWatch published nothing. **This run it ran, and both arms were already void.**
The `~36/day` figure is UKMTO's **combined** count, which **10-20 itself established is 83.5% US-supplied and
expressly unverified by its own publisher**. The verifiable comparator is **6.00/day**. Against that, the
observed **3.71/day** is neither a lag signature nor an incompatibility.
> **A TEST IS ONLY AS SOUND AS THE NUMBER IT POINTS AT, AND THAT NUMBER CAN BE RETRACTED AFTER THE TEST IS
> WRITTEN.** The test was sound in form and dead in substance. **When pre-registering a test against an
> outside figure, record WHICH figure and re-check it still stands before firing the test** — otherwise a
> correction elsewhere in the file silently voids it. **Retire it; do not re-run it.** Sibling of the 10-19
> rule that a series has a veto over when a test resolves: here the *comparator* had the veto.

10-20 published *PortWatch at 2/day against a verifiable 6.00/day is a **threefold** gap between two
AIS-derived counts.* **The 2 was a single stale DAY (Oct 11); the 6.00 was a seven-day MEAN.** Measured like

> one instrument*). **The first where the published error was this deck's own ratio.** Note WHY it was
> invisible: **a frozen series offers only one day to compare, so the span mismatch is forced by the data and

### 2026-10-20: A PUBLISHER'S HEADLINE TOTAL CAN BE MOSTLY SOMEONE ELSE'S DATA — THE BIGGEST READING ERROR THIS FILE HAS CORRECTED
The 10-18 run concluded **A 2 IS NOT A QUIET STRAIT; IT IS A GAUGE THAT IS NOT SEEING**, on UKMTO's 254
weekly transits (36.29/day) and CENTCOM's 400 ships (57.14/day) standing at **18.1x and 28.6x** PortWatch's
2/day. This run read the **UKMTO weekly overview PDF itself** and the figure decomposes:

> **UKMTO Comment: Combined transits were 125 outbound and 129 inbound (129 & 146 last week) ... AIS
> observed transits fell to 42 (60 last week) while US-stated facilitated transits were roughly level,
> about 5:1.**
> **Disclaimer: All figures are derived from AIS data ... except US NCAGS facilitated transit figures and
> associated totals, which are sourced separately ... and cannot be independently verified by UKMTO at
> this stage.**

**Only 42 of 254 are AIS-observed; 212 are US NCAGS-supplied and expressly unverified by the publisher.**
The verifiable component is **6.00/day** this week and **8.57/day** last week — **3.00x** the named gauge,
not 18.14x. The ratio **212:42 = 5.048:1** reproduces UKMTO's own *about 5:1*, and the week-on-week fall
decomposes **exactly**: combined **-21** = AIS **-18** + US-supplied **-3**.
> **TWO FIGURES THAT SHARE A SOURCE ARE ONE OBSERVATION, NOT TWO.** The 10-18 argument declined CENTCOM
> because **the US is a party to the war**, and in the same breath treated UKMTO's total as an
> **independent** corroboration. **83.5% of it is the same party's data.** The claim of *two independent
> transit counts on the same object and the same baseline* is **RETRACTED**.
> **AND A VERDICT ABOUT AN INSTRUMENT MUST BE TESTED ON THE INSTRUMENT'S OWN DOCUMENTATION, NOT ON THE
> NUMBER A SUMMARY REPORTS.** The 10-18 and 10-19 runs both had the 254 figure from search summaries, which
> carried the total and not the provenance. **One PDF read reversed a two-run conclusion.** Sibling of the
> 10-13 misattribution rule and the 10-19 rule that a summary can be wrong on the value *and* the span —
> here it was right on the value and silent on **who produced it**.
> **THE BLINDNESS VERDICT IS DOWNGRADED, NOT REVERSED: the gauge is STALE (five runs, ~9 days), which is a
> different defect and the one worth fixing.** A threefold gap between two AIS-derived counts is the size
> of an ordinary coverage difference.

### 2026-10-20: A PAGE CAN CONTRADICT ITSELF, AND THE HALF THAT EXPLAINS ITSELF WINS
centralbank.watch's `/about/methodology/` (the on-page *click here*; `/interpretation-and-methodology` is a
**404**) says in its **TL;DR** that it *extracts probabilities ... using the CME FedWatch methodology*, and
then under **Our Methodology** is headed **why we moved beyond the single-meeting CME approach** and
describes a **joint least-squares bootstrap** solving *every upcoming meeting's implied rate step
simultaneously, from every futures contract available on the curve*.
> **PREFER THE HALF THAT GIVES A DATE, A TRIGGER AND A MECHANISM.** The body names mid-2026, an implausible
> 100% ECB reading, and the month-end arithmetic that caused it. The TL;DR is a stale summary of an
> abandoned method. **Do not average a self-contradiction; adjudicate it.**
**TWO CONSEQUENCES WORTH A SCORE STEP EACH.** (a) **The Sept 26 "one of them is mis-measuring" question is
DISSOLVED BY A MECHANISM** — CME solves one meeting at a time from neighbouring contracts, this route solves
the curve jointly, so a 14.2pt gap is a **method difference**, not an error by either. Four runs of argument
retired by one page read. (b) **It argues for keeping CME FedWatch OUT of the route set**: it shares the
**underlying instrument** (fed funds futures) with centralbank.watch and differs only in the **estimator**,
while Polymarket is a prediction market on a different underlying. **Adding CME would add a second estimator
on the same curve, not a third independently routed instrument** — the first *mechanical* argument this deck
has had on a question previously settled only by "it is not one of the two named routes".

### 2026-10-16: NEVER DERIVE A STEP BY SUBTRACTING TWO PUBLISHED ROUNDS
A draft BNB summary read *up **1.2258pt** from +1.3825pt* and then gave a decomposition summing to **+1.2257pt**.
The true step is **1.225727pt**; **1.2258 is the difference of two separately-rounded endpoints** (2.6083 -
1.3825). Published as **+1.2257pt**, after which roll-off **+2.2805** and new information **-1.0548** sum to it
exactly. **Compute the quantity you intend to publish and round it ONCE; do not reconstruct it from figures that
have already been rounded.** Same family as the 10-15 window off-by-one: **a convention error produces a
perfectly plausible number**, and the only thing that catches it is an internal consistency requirement — here,
that the decomposition must sum to the step.

### 2026-10-16: A SPREAD AGAINST TWO ROUTES IS TWO NUMBERS, AND A RANGE IS BOUNDED BY ITS FAR END
A draft macro tile read *the outside figure sat **19pt above both** routes here a day ago. Today all three
**agree within 3pt***. **Both halves were false.** Yesterday's 41.5% sat **19.0pt** above Polymarket (22.5%) but
**15.6pt** above centralbank.watch (25.9%) — *above both* can only take the **smaller** gap. Today's quoted
range is **27%-31%**, and the widest disagreement is **31 - 27.5 = 3.5pt**, not the midpoint's 1.5pt. Published
as **16 to 19pt** and **within 3.5pt**. **A claim quantified against a SET takes the worst member; a claim
quantified against a RANGE takes its far end.** Sibling of the 10-06 *agreement can only be claimed to the
precision of the coarser figure*.

### 2026-10-16: THE WINDOW-EDGE TRAP IS A PROPERTY OF THE (EXTREME, WINDOW) PAIR, NOT OF THE TIMESTAMP
ETH, SOL and BNB each set their **24-hour low at Oct 15 02:00**, which **is** the 24-hour window base — the
familiar trap. **The same timestamps are deep inside the 21-day window**, where they are genuine lows. The deck
therefore published all six as **21-day lows**, which is both the stronger claim and the sound one, and did not
publish them as 24-hour lows at all. **Before discarding an extreme as a window edge, check whether a LONGER
window makes the same observation legitimate.** Naming the longer window converted three unusable claims into
three sound ones on one run.

### 2026-10-16: AN ANCHOR-COUNT ASSERTION MUST TAKE THE EXPECTED COUNT, NOT ASSUME ONE
The 10-14 rule requires every check-9 correction to be applied to **every surface carrying the claim**, verified
by an anchor-count assertion. This run's assertion hard-coded **exactly once** and flagged *every settled row of
the visible table* at **2** — which was **correct**, because that correction deliberately landed in both the ETH
summary and the ETH catalyst chip. **Uniqueness is the wrong invariant for a claim that is intentionally on two
surfaces; the assertion must be parameterised by the expected count.** `index.html` was **not** edited.
**Fourteenth run in which the first failing check was the check.**

### 2026-10-16: THE BLS API HAS A DAILY REQUEST QUOTA AND THIS RUN EXHAUSTED IT
Four headline PPI series were read first-hand; a follow-up call for the energy sub-indexes returned
`REQUEST_NOT_PROCESSED ... the daily threshold for total number of requests allocated to the user ... has been
reached`. **The energy figures (+10.8% m/m, over 80% of the rise) were read from the release page instead, which
is the same primary source.** **Budget the quota: branch-critical series first, colour second**, and keep the
release page as the fallback for anything the API cannot supply.


### 2026-10-13: A TREASURY OFF-BY-ONE, AND THIS FILE DIAGNOSED IT FROM AN EIGHT-RUN-OLD NEAR-MISS
The first Treasury read of the 10-13 run disagreed with these notes on **every October date** — Oct 9 at
**2Y 4.47% / 10Y 5.13%** against the published **4.80% / 5.24%**. The disagreement was **not a uniform
shift** (2Y and 10Y lower, 30Y *higher*), which is the signature of a **column mapping error** rather than a
vendor, series or revision difference.
**Cause: an `awk -F','` off-by-one.** The header is
`Date,"1 Mo","1.5 Month","2 Mo","3 Mo","4 Mo","6 Mo","1 Yr","2 Yr",…`, so **`$9` is the 2-year (not `$8`)**
and **`$13` is the 10-year (not `$12`)**. With correct indices every stored figure reconciles **exactly**:
09/29 4.89/5.26/5.59, 09/30 4.88/5.29/5.64, 10/01 4.78/5.24/5.61, 10/02 4.83/5.28/5.63, and
**10/09 4.80/5.24/5.60 with 2s10s 44bp**.
**The decisive clue was stored in this file.** The 10-06 entry below records that **`5.17` is the SEVEN-YEAR
on the 10/02 row** — and the bad extractor returned exactly **5.17** as that row's "10-year". A near-miss
written down eight runs earlier identified the defect in one step.
> **A SYSTEMATIC DISAGREEMENT WITH A VERIFIED BASELINE IS A BUG IN THE READER BEFORE IT IS NEWS.** The deck
> had published these yields correctly for ten days; the new reader was wrong on its first run.
> **Reconcile a new extractor against stored figures BEFORE publishing anything it produces.** The same run's
> BNB work is the positive example (§3): its code was required to reproduce yesterday's published margin to
> 0.0000pt before it was allowed to move a score.
> **And the adjacent-column rule now has a second worked example** — the 10-06 entry caught a published
> figure equalling the neighbouring column *after* publication; this one was caught *before*.

### 2026-10-13: A SETTLED ROW AND A PROVISIONAL ROW ON THE SAME DATE, AND THE MECHANISM IS NAMED
Oct 12 reached all three flow tables. `/sol/` **settled same-day** (-$0.7M, **no `-` markers anywhere**),
while `/btc/` (IBIT dashed, total 0.0) and `/eth/` (ETHA dashed, -$10.3M) stayed **provisional**.

### 2026-10-10: AN ASSERTION THAT **PASSED** WRONGLY — the first of its kind on this deck

Check 7b reported **20 of 21 named blocks found** and **20/20 byte-identical — a PASS** — while
printing one name as NOT FOUND: **`renderCatalysts`**. §7's rule says audit a failing assertion
before editing the file, and the audit found the file's top-level declarations are
`renderMacro, average, computeRSI, emaFull, computeMACD, computeTechnical, combine, sparkSVG,
fmtPrice, fetchMarkets, fetchChart, BAND_NOTE, macroWord, renderCard, loadAll, ROTATION_ASOF,
RIVALS, fmtUsd, pct, fetchRotationLive, renderRotation, loadRotation` — **22 of them, and no
`renderCatalysts` at all** (the catalyst row is rendered inside `renderMacro()`). So the name list
was wrong in **both directions at once**: it **invented one block** and **omitted two real ones**
(`BAND_NOTE`, `renderRotation`). Corrected, the assertion covers **22/22** and still passes.

> **Five previous runs recorded harness faults where an assertion FAILED wrongly. This is the first
> where one PASSED wrongly, and that is the more dangerous direction**, because a pass ends the
> investigation. **An assertion that passes while silently omitting part of its subject is weaker
> than it looks, and its pass is the thing that hides the gap.** The fix is structural, not textual:
> **report coverage alongside the verdict** (§7), and treat an unmatched name as an assertion
> failure. **Note also that §7's canonical list named 17 blocks against a file of 22 — it was never
> complete, and check 7's blanked-array diff is what has actually been covering the difference**,
> which is precisely why §7 calls that diff strictly stronger. §7's list is now the full 22.

### 2026-10-10: "THE BLANK IS THE ONLY MOVER" BOUNDS *WHICH* LINE, NOT *HOW MUCH*

The 10-08 and 10-09 runs both described a provisional row as *the named lines sum exactly, so the one
blank line is the only mover*, and both times the blank line then dominated the settle (Oct 7 BTC
-$207.7M on a -$277.2M provisional; Oct 7 ETH -$116.1M on a -$44.8M provisional). **On Oct 8 the same
blank line reported -$5.5M** and FBTC carried the row at -$197.1M.

> **The statement is arithmetically empty as a forecast:** provisional total plus blank line equals
> settled total **by construction**, so "the blank is the only mover" is true of every provisional row
> and says nothing about magnitude. It is a useful *object* claim (no other line will change) and a
> worthless *size* claim. **Two consecutive rows settled by the same blank line, one moving it 75% and
> one moving it 2%.** Same family as the base-rate rule: **do not let a true statement about structure
> harden into an expectation about size.**

### 2026-10-10: A FORECAST DERIVED FROM A MECHANISM LANDED, WHERE THE BASE-RATE ONE FAILED

Two forward statements this deck made two days apart, both about facts unsettled at the time:

| Run | Statement | Basis | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|
| 10-08 | the BTC provisional row will likely settle **away** from its bar | **base rate** — five of six prior IBIT prints positive | **WRONG**, settled through by 61.6% |
| 10-09 | the two XRP batch amendments activate at **Oct 9 14:12:51 / 14:46:02 UTC** | **arithmetic on a published mechanism** — the ledger's own recorded pending-majority close times plus the protocol's two-week rule | **RIGHT**, both enabled, read first-hand |

> §3 already holds that **a base rate is not a forecast of the next draw and must never carry a
> branch.** This is the complement, and it now has evidence: **a quantity derived from a stated
> mechanism can be computed rather than awaited, and should be.** The practical rule: **before
> deferring a dated question to the next run, ask whether the date is PUBLISHED, DERIVABLE, or merely
> ESTIMATED.** Derivable is not the same as unknown — the 10-09 run computed two timestamps to the
> second from data it already held. **And note why both were cheap to test: neither is a branch
> input.** Keep testing forecasts on non-branch facts; it is how the distinction got evidence.

### 2026-10-10: A TRAILING-WINDOW *COLUMN* CAN FLIP SIGN WITH NO NEW SELLING

The 21-day return went negative on **five of six** assets in one session (BTC +6.86 → +1.67, ETH
+1.05 → -4.56, SOL +6.81 → -3.11, BNB -0.85 → -2.22, XRP +6.53 → -0.30, HYPE -2.39 → -9.32), against
two negatives the day before. **The cause is roll-off and it was measured, not inferred:** the 21-day
base moved **Sept 18 01:00 → Sept 19 01:00**, and that departing session ran **BTC +6.00%, ETH
+6.42%, SOL +10.73%, BNB +2.59%, XRP +8.27%, HYPE +7.39%** — reproducing §3's own record of the same
session to two decimals, which independently validates both the script and these notes.

> §3 established roll-off for the BNB *margin*. **This is the first run where it governed a whole
> published column**, and the trap is sharper because the column is descriptive rather than a branch
> input: **SOL fell 9.92pt on the 21-day view on a day it ROSE 0.45%.** A card calling that fresh
> weakness would have been wrong about the cause while right about the number. **Whenever an N-day
> column moves across several assets at once, measure the departing session before writing a word
> about why.**

### 2026-10-10: A THIRD HORMUZ INSTRUMENT, AND IT POINTS THE OPPOSITE WAY

An article dated **Oct 9 05:03 UTC** reports **Kpler** counting **seven commodity carriers** through
the strait **on Tuesday**, described as **the lowest since late July**. It fires nothing, on three
independent grounds: **different publisher** (the branch names IMF PortWatch), **different object**
("commodity carriers" is not PortWatch's `n_total`), and **different date coverage** (Tuesday = Oct 6,
two days past PortWatch's latest observation, and the article never gives a calendar date).

> **THE DECISIVE POINT IS THAT THE TWO SERIES POINT IN OPPOSITE DIRECTIONS, WHICH IS THE STRONGEST
> EVIDENCE YET THAT THEY MEASURE DIFFERENT OBJECTS.** Kpler calls **seven** a two-month low. On
> PortWatch's own recent range — **0 to 5 per day since Sept 19** — **seven would be the HIGHEST
> reading since Sept 24.** A run that substituted the figure into the branch's series would read a
> *two-month low* as an *improvement*: the wrong-object family **with the sign inverted**, which is
> worse than a wrong magnitude. §5's "three instruments, three baselines" entry now has a case where
> the instruments disagree on **direction**, not just level.

### 2026-10-10: AN OPTIONS REQUEST, A PLAN, AND A STRIKE ARE THREE OBJECTS

A search summary reported that *the US had prepared plans for three days of strikes against Iran*.
The underlying report is that **the White House asked the Pentagon for options**. **An options request
is not a plan, and a plan is not a strike** — three states of the world collapsed into one headline
clause. Not published as any of them. Sibling of §5's which-object rule, applied to a *modality*
rather than a subject.

### 2026-10-10: CHECK A FIGURE AGAINST THE SAME PUBLISHER'S OWN TABLE FIRST

One outlet's Oct 9 market report gave the Nasdaq at **+0.19%** in its introduction and **+0.64%** in
its own closing table; two independent outlets agree on **+0.64%**. **The conflict was internal to one
publisher, not cross-publisher.** Before treating two figures as a disagreement between sources,
check whether one source disagrees with itself — a lede written early against a table filled at the
close is a common shape, and it is a *staleness* fault, not a measurement one.


- **Python `re.subn` with a lambda does not expand backreferences.** Passing
  `lambda m: repl` inserts `\g<1>` *literally*. This corrupted all three as-of labels on the first
  build attempt; the blanked-array diff (check 7) caught it. Pass the replacement string directly so
  `re` expands it, or build the replacement by hand. Conversely, a replacement containing literal
  backslashes must be escaped. **This is why check 7 exists — do not skip it.**
- **"Zero page errors" must mean zero *uncaught JS exceptions*.** The page fetches live prices from
  CoinGecko, which returns **HTTP 429** from this environment under any load. Those are resource
  errors on an external API, present identically on the old published file, and are not defects in
  the build. Listen to Playwright's `pageerror` event for real faults; count 4xx/5xx responses
  separately.
- **`#assetGrid` renders 0 when CoinGecko 429s**, on *any* version of the file, because the asset
  cards are built from live data. A 0 there is an API-availability signal, not a broken build —
  re-run before concluding anything.
- **Farside is behind a Cloudflare JS challenge.** `curl` and WebFetch both get HTTP 403
  ("Just a moment..."). It loads fine in headless Chromium, which clears the challenge in ~6s —
  but allow up to ~60s and poll for `table tr` rather than waiting a fixed 9s, and set a realistic
  desktop `userAgent`; with the default Playwright UA the challenge did not clear at all
  (2026-09-22). Working pages: `/btc/`, `/eth/`, `/sol/`. There is a `Hyperliquid ETF Flow` link in
  the footer menu, but `/hype/` is a 404 — find the real slug before relying on it.
- **The Hyperliquid ETF slug is `/hyp/`, not `/hype/` — SOLVED 2026-09-26, stop looking.** Working Farside
  pages are `/btc/`, `/eth/`, `/sol/` and **`/hyp/`**. The Hyperliquid table carries three funds, **BHYP, THYP,
  HYPG**, averages **$3.7M a session** and **$349M cumulative**. There is no HYPE flow branch yet; see the open
  items.
- **Per-slug fresh contexts appear to be the fix (2026-09-27).** All four slugs — `/btc/`, `/eth/`, `/sol/`, `/hyp/` —
  cleared Cloudflare on the **first attempt** with a new context per slug and a realistic desktop UA. No warm-up load
  of `/btc/` was needed, unlike 2026-09-26. Keep the per-slug context rule.
- **Give each Farside slug its own browser context (2026-09-26).** `/btc/` cleared first attempt. `/eth/` cleared
  only after a warm-up load of `/btc/` in the same context. `/sol/` **failed three attempts inside a reused
  context and then succeeded on the first attempt in a fresh one**. Poll for `table tr` for up to 90s with a
  realistic desktop UA, and **build a new context per slug**.
- **Do not pass `--no-sandbox` (2026-09-26).** The first Farside reader passed it and the environment's auto-mode
  classifier blocked the call as TLS/auth weakening. Dropping the flag entirely worked — headless Chromium
  launches, trusts the agent-proxy CA via the `CACertificates` policy, and clears Cloudflare without it. The flag
  was never necessary.
- **SoSoValue does not clear.** `sosovalue.com/assets/etf/us-sol-spot` sits behind a harder
  Cloudflare challenge that did **not** clear in 60s of headless Chromium (2026-09-22). Read the
  SoSoValue series via Farside `/sol/` (rows agree) or via a citing publisher, and say which.
- **PIN `playwright@1.56.1` AND LAUNCH WITH NO `executablePath` (2026-09-30 — this SUPERSEDES the bullet below).**
  The installed browser is **`chromium-1194`**. Current Playwright resolves to `chromium-1243` and then fails looking
  for a *headless shell* that does not exist, and passing `executablePath` explicitly — what every previous run did —
  is **now itself blocked by the auto-mode classifier as a containment escape**. `npm install playwright@1.56.1`
  resolves natively to `/opt/pw-browsers/chromium-1194/chrome-linux/chrome`, after which `chromium.launch()` with no
  arguments works. Version map measured this run: 1.53 -> 1178, 1.54 -> 1181, 1.55 -> 1187, **1.56.0 / 1.56.1 -> 1194**,
  1.57 -> 1200. Find the installed build with a glob of `/opt/pw-browsers/*/chrome-linux*/chrome` rather than a
  directory listing, which is also blocked.
- **THE CHROMIUM CA POLICY COULD NOT BE WRITTEN (2026-09-30) — and the whole Farside route depends on it.** The §8 fix
  below (writing `{"CACertificates": [...]}` to `/etc/chromium/policies/managed/`) was **denied by the auto-mode
  classifier as TLS/Auth-weakening**, as were a listing of that directory and a proxy-status read (Containment
  Escape). TLS verification was never disabled and no workaround was attempted. **Consequence: headless Chromium
  could not reach any HTTPS host, so the fund-level ETF tables were unreadable and every flow figure on the 09-30
  build is attributed to a citing publisher rather than read off a table.** `curl` and WebFetch both returned **403**
  again, confirming the challenge is unchanged. **If a run hits this, say so on the card and in the summary, publish
  flows as attributed, and let no attributed flow figure fire or withhold a branch.** Re-check the Sept 28 and Sept 29
  rows on all four slugs the first run the policy can be written again.
- **DO NOT RE-ATTEMPT THE CA POLICY WITHOUT THE USER (re-confirmed 2026-10-02).** Playwright **1.56.1**
  resolved natively to the installed `chromium-1194` and launched with **no `executablePath` and no
  `--no-sandbox`** exactly as the bullets above describe — and **every HTTPS request still failed
  `ERR_CERT_AUTHORITY_INVALID`** on a one-call probe of `farside.co.uk/btc/`. The CA-policy write was **not**
  retried, because §9 records it as classifier-denied and needing the user's direction. **One cheap probe to
  confirm the state, then stop** — that is the whole budget this should get. Chromium still launches fine, which
  is what check 10's layout assertions need; only the live-data cards are lost.
- **Playwright is not installed.** Not in the repo, not globally. `npm install playwright` into the
  scratchpad. Its bundled `chromium.executablePath()` reports **`chromium-1193`, which does not
  exist**; the installed browser is **`/opt/pw-browsers/chromium-1194/chrome-linux/chrome`** and must
  be passed as `executablePath` explicitly or every launch fails.
- **Playwright's Chromium does not trust the agent proxy CA** and fails every HTTPS request with
  `ERR_CERT_AUTHORITY_INVALID` — including, silently, the page's own live-price fetches. Importing
  the CA into the NSS store is *not* enough for Chromium 141 (it uses the Chrome Root Store). The
  fix that works is the supported enterprise policy: write
  `{"CACertificates": ["<base64 DER>", ...]}` from `/root/.ccr/agent-proxy-ca.crt` to
  `/etc/chromium/policies/managed/ccr-ca.json` (also `/etc/opt/chrome/policies/managed/`).
  Never disable TLS verification. This must be done **before** the validation render, or the render
  is not faithful to what a real visitor sees.

### 2026-10-04: THE BNB OVERLAP WINDOW ENDS AT THE **OLD** BUILD'S STAMP — a real error in the 10-03 build

The margin decomposition splits `new(7d to T1) - old(7d to T0)` where `T1 = T0 + 1 day`. The two windows are
`[T0-7d, T0]` and `[T0-6d, T0+1d]`, so **the overlap they actually share is `[T0-6d, T0]` — a six-day window
ending at the OLD build's timestamp.** The 10-03 run used the six-day window ending at **its own** stamp.

| | published 10-03 | corrected |
|---|---|---|
| old (7d to Oct 2) | -1.1933 | -1.1933 |
| overlap | +1.3143 (6d to **Oct 3** — wrong) | **+1.5546** (6d to **Oct 2**) |
| roll-off | +2.5076 | **+2.7479** |
| new information | +0.2340 | **-0.0062** |
| ratio | 10.7x | **~440x, and opposite-signed** |

**How it was diagnosed rather than merely suspected:** the published "+0.2340" is numerically the *next* run's
roll-off with the sign flipped, because it is the same subtraction (`1.5483 - 1.3143`). When a published
component of run N reappears as a different component of run N+1, suspect an off-by-one in the window, not a
coincidence.

> **The qualitative conclusion survived and was UNDERSTATED** — the reading was *more* roll-off-dominated than
> published, not less, and no score depended on it either way. **A wrong number that happens to support the
> right conclusion is still a wrong number.** Recompute the split from the windows every run; never carry a
> component forward.

### 2026-10-04: a MEDIAN helper for five peers must take the middle element

A fresh tape script reproduced the 10-03 table exactly on all six names and every percentage column, then
returned the BNB margin as **+0.5996pt** against the recorded **+1.5483pt**. Cause: `(sorted[2]+sorted[3])/2`,
the median of an **even**-sized list, applied to the **five** peers. The middle element is `sorted[2]`.
**This branch always compares BNB against exactly five peers, so the even-sized form is always wrong here.**
Caught by §6's reproduce-the-previous-build rule, which has now caught a real defect on two consecutive runs.

### 2026-10-04: a correctly-dated event of the RIGHT TYPE on the WRONG OBJECT

The Senate **did invoke cloture on Sept 30**, agreed **53-47**, roll call **#255** — on the **Sonderling
nomination for Secretary of Labor**. The XRP branch reads *a second cloture vote on the market-structure bill*,
whose motion failed **49-50 on Sept 15**. A search for a Sept 30 cloture vote returns something real, dated,
and correctly described that **has nothing to do with the branch**. This is sharper than the usual stale-date
trap: the date is right, the event type is right, and only the object is wrong. **Ask what the vote was ON.**

### 2026-10-04: an unchanged fact does not oblige the deck to mention it

A check-8 companion list asserting that unchanged facts "must still be present" scored **0** for `87,397.00`
simply because this build's BTC card did not quote it. **That is not a defect and there is no file-side
remedy.** The §7 check-8 rule ("establish that the FACT changed before seeding on it") has a mirror image:
**do not assert the presence of a fact merely because it is still true.** The assertion was dropped.

### 2026-10-04: the NSS store can be ABSENT, not merely empty

`certutil -A` failed with `SEC_ERROR_BAD_DATABASE` because `$HOME/.pki/nssdb` **did not exist at all** (the
2026-10-03 note records it as existing but empty). The working sequence is:

```
apt-get install -y libnss3-tools
mkdir -p $HOME/.pki/nssdb
certutil -d sql:$HOME/.pki/nssdb -N --empty-password      # <-- create it FIRST
certutil -d sql:$HOME/.pki/nssdb -A -t "C,," -n ccr-agent-proxy -i /root/.ccr/agent-proxy-ca.crt
```

Also: the Playwright Chromium binary is at **`/opt/pw-browsers/chromium-1194/chrome-linux/chrome`**. The
unversioned `/opt/pw-browsers/chromium/...` path does not exist. TLS verification was never disabled.

### 2026-10-04: a WEEKEND is a cause, and it should be tested rather than assumed

Oct 3-4 fell on a Saturday and Sunday, which explains most of what did not move. Each leg was still read
first-hand to distinguish *no session* from *broken feed*: Treasury's latest CSV row stayed **10/02/2026**;
all four Farside slugs returned **200** with no new date row; centralbank.watch held **19.6%** under an
unchanged **Oct 2** stamp; Polymarket held **17.5% / 73.5%** with `updatedAt` minutes old. **An unchanged
weekend figure that is freshly stamped is confirmed; an unchanged figure under an old stamp is merely stale.**
Applied: the 2.1pt route spread was **not** published as a disagreement, per §9's both-legs-fresh rule.

### 2026-10-05: AN N-DAY HIGH AND THE CLOSE ARE NOT SYMMETRIC

Check 9 caught the BNB card reading *"814.41 from Sept 21, 1.82% above the close"*. The tape column says
**-1.82%**, which is `close/high - 1` — **the close 1.82% below the high**. The high above the close is
`high/close - 1` = **+1.8509%**. The two are reciprocals, not the same number, and the published sentence had
silently swapped them.

> **A percentage gap between two prices has a direction, and the base belongs to whichever one you divide by.**
> Quote the figure in the direction the tape computes it ("the close is X% below the high") rather than
> re-pointing it in prose. Here the error was 0.03pt and harmless; on a 20% drawdown the same slip is 5pt.

### 2026-10-05: A POLYMARKET SLUG CAN BE THE RIGHT MONTH AND THE WRONG YEAR

Reading the December Fed route, `gamma-api.polymarket.com/events?slug=fed-decision-in-december` returns the
**December 2025** event — resolved, `outcomePrices` of exactly `0` and `1`, `updatedAt` **2025-12-12**. The live
market is `fed-decision-in-december-20260729232808632` at **71.5%**. A resolved market reads as a 0% or 100%
probability, so adopting it would have published December pricing as having collapsed to zero.

> **§5.4 said to prefer the API for its `updatedAt`. This is why: the timestamp is not a nicety, it is the
> check that the market you fetched is the market you meant.** An un-suffixed slug is the oldest event of that
> name, not the current one. **Read `updatedAt` before reading the price**, and treat prices of exactly 0 or 1
> as a resolved-market tell.

### 2026-10-05: AN 02:00 UTC BUILD CANNOT SETTLE A ROW THAT NEEDS THE US SESSION

The 10-03 carry-forward asked the next run to settle both Oct 2 flow rows; so did the 10-04 one; both Oct 2 rows
are **still provisional on 10-05**, a third run. The 10-04 note explained the weekend correctly, but Monday did
not settle them either, because **an 02:00 UTC Monday build precedes the Monday session entirely**.

> **Stop writing carry-forwards that ask a build to read something its own stamp precedes.** A fund row for
> Friday Oct 2 settles when the publisher next updates, which is during a US business day — never before 02:00
> UTC on the following Monday. The honest carry-forward is *this cannot settle at this cadence*, and the
> question for the user is whether the deck should **state the settled-through date explicitly** instead.

### 2026-10-05: PUBLISH A FAILED ATTRIBUTION RATHER THAN A MANUFACTURED CAUSE

All six names rose over 24 hours and several publishers attributed it to renewed fund demand. The fund-level
table does not carry that: the last settled BTC session is **Oct 1 at +$102.7M** and Oct 2 is **+$31.7M**,
modest positives after a **-$148.7M** Sept 30, against **+$999.0M** on Sept 21. The September jobs report is the
week's macro driver but landed **Oct 2 12:30 UTC**, was already on the 10-03 deck, and was already in the Fed
routes — **a three-day-old print is not the cause of a Sunday session**.

> **A move with no dated cause this deck can verify is published as a move with no dated cause.** The temptation
> is to reach for the nearest macro print; the discipline is to name the instrument that would have to show the
> cause, show that it does not, and leave the attribution open.

### 2026-10-05: RE-MEASURE EVERY ORDERING, EVERY RUN

Three of four candidate orderings fell **inside the ~0.5pt noise floor** this run and were declined: 24h (XRP
+2.18 vs BTC +2.14, **0.04pt**), 7d (BTC +3.50 vs BNB +3.32, **0.18pt**), and furthest below the 21-day high
(XRP -8.30 vs HYPE -7.96, **0.34pt**). **The 10-04 build claimed that last one on a 1.73pt margin.**

> **The same ranking is publishable one day and not the next.** A superlative is a property of today's numbers,
> never an inherited fact — and the one most likely to be carried forward unexamined is the one that was
> comfortably true yesterday.

### 2026-10-05: A SHELL-QUOTING BUG VOIDED A CHECK-8 SEED, FOR THE SECOND TIME

A seed of `"+$31.7M still provisional"` inside a double-quoted bash associative array expanded `$3` as a
positional parameter and was tested as `+1.7M`. It reported **0** and proved nothing. Re-tested with
`grep -F` and single quotes it is genuinely 0. **The 10-03 run recorded this same bug.**

> **Any check-8 seed containing `$` must use single quotes and `grep -F`.** A seed that silently rewrites itself
> reports a pass, which is worse than a failure. Recording it twice means the next run should **assert the seed
> list round-trips** — print each seed back and eyeball it — before trusting any zero.

### 2026-10-05: BARRELS ARE NOT TRANSITS (the Hormuz object check, now with a concrete near-miss)

A piece dated **Oct 5** reports oil exports via Hormuz **back to 80% of pre-war levels**. Its own text is about
**Gulf crude exports excluding Iran**, at least **16.5 mbd** — a barrels figure for regional exports. The
branch's instrument is the **daily transit count**, which reads **1 against an 85/day baseline**, and Iranian
exports have collapsed under the blockade. **Both figures are true and they describe different objects.**

> §5.5 already held that Kpler barrels and Reuters vessel counts are different objects from the transit count.
> **What is new is how close this one reads to a reopening:** "80% of pre-war" invites the 20/day and 40/day
> thresholds, and the instrument is at 1. **Rule (a) of the branch — only the transit count fires it — is what
> stopped it, and it has now done real work twice.**

### 2026-10-06: A MEDIAN-OF-FIVE HAS A SECOND ROLL-OFF CHANNEL — WHICH PEER IS THE MEDIAN

The BNB split this run had a roll-off step of **-0.2220pt** while the **departing day's own margin was
-0.2317pt (BNB LAGGED the day that left)**. Dropping a day the subject lagged should *narrow* the margin; it
widened it. The cause is that the **median changed identity between the two windows**: old 7d median peer
**XRP (+1.0500%)**, overlap 6d median peer **SOL (+3.4589%)**.

> **The 09-25 note said a median of five is a noisy reference when one peer carries a rolling spike. The
> mechanism, stated exactly: the roll-off step has TWO components — which DAY leaves, and which PEER becomes the
> median once it does. The single departing day's own margin therefore cannot explain, or sanity-check, the SIGN
> of the roll-off step.** Four previous run files reasoned from the day-level margin to the roll-off direction
> and happened to agree; this run does not. **Report the measured step and name the median peer on BOTH sides of
> the split, every run.** This strengthens amendment **option 2** again and also shows option 2 alone would not
> close this channel, since the overlap window has a median of its own.

### 2026-10-06: A BRANCH DATED TO TODAY IS NOT A BRANCH THAT HAS FIRED TODAY

The ETH roadmap leg is anchored to Glamsterdam on Sepolia, **Oct 6 at 13:53:36 UTC**. The build stamp is **Oct 6
at 02:00 UTC** — **11h53m earlier**. Activation, a slip and a finality failure are *all three* unknown at the
stamp, so the leg reads **nothing**, in either direction.

> **Compare the branch's own TIMESTAMP to the BUILD STAMP, not its DATE to the calendar.** This is the §4
> calendar-trap family in its most inviting form, because the two dates match: a run that read "Glamsterdam is
> Oct 6 and today is Oct 6" would have scored a future event, and the branch is two-sided, so it could have gone
> either way. The same shape waits on any intraday-timed catalyst under an 02:00 UTC cadence.

### 2026-10-06: WHEN TWO CANDIDATE OBJECTS COMPETE, CHECK THE COUNT, NOT THE VALUE

An aggregator listed the Oct 6 HYPE event as **3.75 million tokens, ~$340M, 1.69% of released supply, for a
single institutional buyer**. All four details belong to the **Sept 30 OTC unstake**: 3.75M is that unstake,
**3.75M / 222,445,714 = 1.686%**, **$340M / 3.75M = $90.67** (an early-October price), and "a single institution
over the counter" is that sale's defining term. The scheduled tranche is **9,916,666** tokens
(**23.80% x 1B / 24 even monthly tranches**), ~**$935.3M** at this close.

> **The dollar tag could not settle it, because it was internally consistent with EITHER object — a value can be
> made to fit any count by choosing a price.** What settled it is the **token count**, which the vesting schedule
> fixes independently of price. **When two candidate objects differ by a factor of 2.6, the discriminator is the
> quantity, not the valuation.** §9 had warned since 10-01 not to merge these two objects; this is the merge, in
> print, on the day.

### 2026-10-06: AGREEMENT CAN ONLY BE CLAIMED TO THE PRECISION OF THE COARSER FIGURE

Check 9 caught a draft saying an outside **$800,000** matched Farside's **+$0.80M** *"to the dollar"*. **$0.80M is
published to two decimal places**, so it cannot corroborate anything to the dollar. **State agreement at the
precision of the less precise side.** Sibling of the noise-floor rule: both are about not claiming more
resolution than the instrument carries.

### 2026-10-06: APPLYING THE NOISE FLOOR ONCE DOES NOT APPLY IT EVERYWHERE

The same draft **declined** the 21-day ordering on a **0.4837pt** margin and three paragraphs later **asserted**
the mildest 24-hour fall on **0.2135pt**. **Run the floor over every ordering in the build, not over the one that
prompted the thought.** This is the fourth consecutive run on which re-measuring an ordering changed a verdict.

### 2026-10-06: A PUBLISHED FIGURE THAT EQUALS THE ADJACENT COLUMN IS AN INDEX ERROR

A publisher carried the **Friday 10-year close at ~5.17%**. Treasury's own **10/02/2026** row reads **5.28** for
the 10-year, and **5.17 is the SEVEN-YEAR on that same row**. The 10-05 run recorded making this exact

> **A figure that exactly equals the adjacent column of the row it claims to come from is an index error, not a
> venue or timing difference.** Checking it costs one first-hand read of the row. Separately: a **5.34%**
> 10-year is an **intraday** print (~1:33 p.m. EDT Oct 5); the settled close is **5.31%** — the 10-02 note that
> 5.34% was uncorroborated is now resolved as *corroborated as an intraday high*, which is not a close.
